name: Grih Darshan / PoliceSoft thana master (Home Department, Bihar) — SOAP web service
publisher: Department of Home (Police), Government of Bihar; NIC Bihar
caveats: Internal government system, not a citizen-facing directory; registration is performed by the SHO under OTP verification
Every SOAP property is individually encrypted client-side (Encriptor.Encrypt with a per-call random salt) behind an Authenticate/token call
.nic.in host blocked by this sandbox's egress proxy; the service itself was never contacted
Calling it without permission would engage IT Act s.43(b)/s.66 per legal-ethics R6 — do not attempt
SHO_Mobile_Num may be a personal mobile, not a post-attached official number
evidence: Endpoint and method names read verbatim from fetched source: raw.githubusercontent.com/patnaapp/GrihDarshan_WithDatabase/master/app/src/main/java/bih/nic/in/policesoft/web_services/WebServiceHelper.java lines 86-108 (SERVICENAMESPACE, SERVICEURL1, GetRangeList, GetPoliceDistrictList, GetSub_DivisionList, Register_Thana_Signup, UpdateThana, Insert_Outpost, Insert_Contact, Authenticate, GetContactList_New, GetMajorUtilitiesList, GetOfficesList). Per-thana field list read from entity/UpdateThanaModel.java and entity/PoliceUser_Details.java: Range_Code, PSCode, Police_Dist_Code, Sub_Div_Code, Thana_Name, SHO_Name, SHO_Mobile_Num, Email_Address, Landline_Num, Thana_Address, Thana_Notification_Avail, Notification_Num, Notification_Date, Land_Avail, Khata_Num, Kheshra_Num, Latitude, Longitude, Photo1, Imei_Num. Outposts carry OutPost_Inch_Name/SHOMobile/SHOEmail (entity/OutPostEntry.java). Play Store id bih.nic.in.policesoft, publisher described as Home Department Govt of Bihar, 'GIS mapping of major utilities and offices under the home department' (search extract; store blocked).
how_to_obtain: Do not scrape. Cite it by name in RTI drafts 5(b) and 5(f) in rti-playbook.md: naming the system, the host and the field list defeats the standard s.7(9) 'we would have to create a new record' refusal. Ask for station-level administrative fields with any officer particulars REDACTED under s.10.
notes: The single most valuable find in this dossier. It proves Bihar holds SHO name, mobile and email per thana in a named electronic system, plus the gazette notification number/date constituting each thana and khata/khesra cadastral parcel numbers for the station building. A second commented-out endpoint, https://www.fts.bih.nic.in/PoliceSoftwebservice.asmx, appears in the same file and is a seed lead.

name: INDIA_POLICE_STATIONS.geojson — national police station point layer
publisher: MHA-derived (feature ids police_station_mha.N), via datta07/INDIAN-SHAPEFILES, mirrored by yashveeeeeeer/india-geodata
time_latest: unknown (repo mirror; jurisdictions sibling dataset dated 2024-08-15)
license: see source repo (jurisdictions sibling is CC0-1.0; stations licence unstated)
caveats: Carries NO officer name, rank, phone or email — the full property set is exactly: state, state_cd, district, district_c, ps, ps_cd, latitude, longitude
District field uses POLICE districts, not revenue districts: Bihar shows 44, against 38 revenue districts
Patna shows 70 stations; Wikipedia's Patna Police article says 75 — neither is authoritative, reconcile against BPRD DoPO
Vintage unstated; new thanas notified since the snapshot will be missing
Point is the station building, not its jurisdiction
evidence: Downloaded 2026-09-20: 5,269,146 bytes. Parsed with python json: 16,459 features. Union of property keys across ALL features is exactly ['district','district_c','latitude','longitude','ps','ps_cd','state','state_cd']. 36 distinct state values. BIHAR = 929 features across 44 district values (PATNA 70, GAYA 47, MOTHIHARI 40, NALANDA 35, MADHUBANI 34); zero Bihar features missing coordinates. Largest states: TAMIL NADU 2427, UTTAR PRADESH 1713, MADHYA PRADESH 1110, MAHARASHTRA 1086, KARNATAKA 1046, ANDHRA PRADESH 1031. Sample: {'state':'BIHAR','state_cd':5,'district':'ARARIA','district_c':5140,'ps':'ARARIA','ps_cd':5140003,'latitude':26.1358,'longitude':87.4659}.
notes: This is the ceiling of what is openly available at national scale, and it is the spine of the 'who polices here' surface. Its total absence of any officer field is itself the headline finding for Part A. Ingest first: one GET, zero personal data, national coverage.

name: police.uk neighbourhood team endpoint — GET /{force}/{neighbourhood}/people
publisher: Home Office / UK Police (data.police.uk)
caveats: Names officers, but on a surface entirely separate from crime data — no crime endpoint carries any officer field
In the publisher's own worked example, contact_details is {} (empty) for BOTH named officers
The usable contact is one level up on the neighbourhood resource: telephone 101 and a team mailbox, not a personal line
bio is free HTML written by the officer; no currency guarantee and no 'as on' date
data.police.uk is EGRESS_BLOCKED in this sandbox; verified against a committed verbatim mirror of the official docs
evidence: Official docs mirrored verbatim at raw.githubusercontent.com/EduardoTrevino/Fail-TaLMs/main/api_docs/OpenData/datapoliceuk.txt (56,174 bytes), fetched 2026-09-20. Example response at lines 898-914 returns objects of {bio, contact_details, name, rank} — 'Andy Cooper'/'Sgt' and 'Andy Price'/'Sgt', both with "contact_details": {}. Documented contact_details keys (lines 921-929): telephone, email, mobile, fax, address, web, facebook, twitter, google-plus, forum, e-messaging, blog, rss. Neighbourhood-level contact_details at lines 793-797: {twitter, facebook, telephone '101', email 'centralleicester.npa@leicestershire.pnn.police.uk'}. Street-level crime response (lines 222-256) has fields category, location_type, location{latitude,street{id,name},longitude}, context, outcome_status, persistent_id, id, location_subtype, month — no officer field. Cross-checked against rkhleics/police-api-client-python docs/reference/neighbourhoods/officers.rst (name, rank, bio, contact_details as dict e.g. {telephone, website}) and tjcain/ukpolice neighbourhood.go/force.go structs.
notes: The design rule to copy: 'what happened here' and 'who polices here' are two endpoints sharing a geography and nothing else. Naming is confined to the second, where an officer is a contact point, never a denominator.

name: police.uk force senior officers endpoint — GET /forces/{force}/people
publisher: Home Office / UK Police (data.police.uk)
caveats: Chief-officer tier only, not station commanders
In the official example contact_details is just a Twitter URL
data.police.uk EGRESS_BLOCKED; verified via mirrored official docs
evidence: Mirrored docs lines 146-171: request https://data.police.uk/api/forces/leicestershire/people, response objects carry bio, contact_details, name, rank; the worked example's contact_details is {"twitter":"http://www.twitter.com/ACCCLeicsPolice"}. Force resource itself carries telephone '0116 222 2222' and engagement_methods (facebook, twitter).
notes: The UK's closest analogue to naming a DGP/IG/SP — force leadership, not the officer in charge of a station.

name: RTI Act 2005 s.4(1)(b)(ix)-(x) — suo motu duty to publish a directory of officers and employees
publisher: Parliament of India
caveats: Exact clause numbering not confirmed against primary text; indiacode.nic.in is EGRESS_BLOCKED
s.8(1)(j) was amended by DPDP Act s.44(3), understood to remove the larger-public-interest override — so RTI is now WEAKER for personal particulars even though s.4 still mandates the directory
Compliance with s.4 is patchy in practice; a published directory may be years out of date
evidence: Search extracts (DoPT 'Disclosure Under Sec. 4(1)(b) of RTI Act, 2005'; MHA 'Information under Section 4(1)(b) of RTI Act, 2005'; righttoinformation.wiki): s.4(1)(b)(ix) requires 'a directory of its officers and employees'; s.4(1)(b)(x) requires 'the monthly remuneration received by each of its officers and employees, including the system of compensation as provided in its regulations'. Seventeen categories, to be published in electronic form where possible and updated at least once a year. Pages not opened (.gov.in blocked).
how_to_obtain: Cite it as the legal basis of RTI draft 5(f) in rti-playbook.md — frame the ask as compliance with an existing statutory obligation, not a novel demand.
notes: The load-bearing provision for Part B: it is the 'obligation under any law to make such personal data publicly available' that engages DPDP s.3(c)(ii)(B) for officer names. It is also the reason we can obtain the OFFICE's contact particulars without touching s.8(1)(j).

name: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii) as applied to police officer directories
publisher: Parliament of India / MeitY
caveats: Primary text not opened — meity.gov.in and dpdpa.com both EGRESS_BLOCKED
Whether the exemption travels to a downstream re-publisher is UNRESOLVED (legal-ethics Blocker 3); no Board decision, no judgment
DPDP has no public-figure carve-out and NO sensitive-personal-data category at all
DPDP has NO journalism exemption, unlike GDPR Art. 85
The argument weakens sharply the moment a name is joined to a crime count, because that creates a new assertion no public authority published
evidence: Search extracts (india-briefing; dpdpa.com s.3 page; Law School Policy Review Jan 2026): the Act does not apply to personal data made publicly available by the Data Principal, or by another person under a legal obligation to make it publicly available; commentary notes the exemption does not extend to combining public data with non-public data or to uses beyond reasonable expectations. Pages not opened.
notes: Position for counsel: s.3(c)(ii)(B) is read together with RTI s.4(1)(b)(ix), which puts the police force under a statutory obligation to publish an officer directory. DPDP is therefore probably NOT our binding constraint on officer names — BNS s.356 and staleness are.
how_to_obtain: Read the bare Act from meity.gov.in or the gazette from an unblocked machine; confirm the exact wording of s.3(c)(ii)(A)-(B) and any illustration before counsel relies on it. Watch Data Protection Board decisions from Nov 2025 onward for the downstream-re-publisher question.

name: Prakash Singh v Union of India (2006) — Directive 3, minimum two-year tenure for SHO in charge of a police station
publisher: Supreme Court of India
caveats: indiankanoon.org EGRESS_BLOCKED; judgment text not read
Compliance is widely reported as partial; the directive is the de jure floor, not the de facto position
Some states legislated equivalents (Punjab Police Act s.15: assured one year extendable to three) — Bihar's position unknown
evidence: Search extracts: 'Police Officers on operational duties in the field like the Inspector General of Police in-charge Zone, Deputy Inspector General of Police in-charge Range, Superintendent of Police in-charge district and Station House Officer in-charge of a Police Station shall have a prescribed minimum tenure of two years unless it is found necessary to remove them prematurely following disciplinary proceedings.' Seven directives issued 22 September 2006, to be operationalised by 31 December 2006.
notes: The benchmark against which RTI draft 5(g) measures actual churn. 'This station has had 9 officers in charge since 2021, against a Supreme Court direction prescribing two years' is a publishable institutional finding that names nobody.
how_to_obtain: Read the judgment on indiankanoon or SCC from an unblocked machine and quote Directive 3 verbatim before it is cited in RTI draft 5(g) or in published copy.

name: Bihar SHO / police officer transfer orders, May-September 2026 (churn evidence)
publisher: Department of Home, Government of Bihar; district Superintendents of Police (reported in Indian media)
caveats: All source pages EGRESS_BLOCKED; figures are from search-result extracts only
Media counts are per-order, not cumulative; no denominator is published with them
Only one of the five orders is specifically an SHO (thanadhyaksh) order — the rest are SDPO/DSP/ASP/BPS tiers
A single district-day observation is not a churn rate; it bounds one from below
evidence: Search extracts: 15 Sep 2026 — 20 SHOs transferred in Patna district in one order (ETV Bharat; Rituraj Kumar Singh appointed SHO of Pataliputra PS); 6 Sep 2026 — 37 SDPO/DSP/ASP transferred by the Home Department; 29 Aug 2026 — 27 Bihar Police Service officers, Notification No. 10560; 18 Aug 2026 — 9 officers; 20 May 2026 — 8 officers. Against Patna's establishment of ~70 stations (INDIA_POLICE_STATIONS.geojson, VERIFIED_LIVE) or 75 (Wikipedia, Patna Police), the 15 Sep order moved roughly 27% of a district's station commanders in a day.
how_to_obtain: RTI draft 5(g) in rti-playbook.md — changes of charge per station with dates, no names — converts this anecdote into a measured distribution.
notes: Planning estimate for Phase 2: assume 30-60% annual turnover of Bihar's 929 SHO postings, lumpy rather than uniform. An annually refreshed SHO name column would be ~40% wrong before it is replaced. This is the decisive technical fact behind the recommendation not to publish names.

name: Delhi Police 'Know Your Police Station' (KYPS) lookup
publisher: Delhi Police
caveats: EGRESS_BLOCKED (.gov.in) — page never opened; shape inferred from the product name and from third-party republications of Delhi SHO/DO name-and-phone lists
Form-gated: one record per query, no bulk export, no API observed
No 'as on' date observed in any republication
evidence: URL returned by WebSearch with title 'Know Your Police Station'. Page not opened (.gov.in blocked).
how_to_obtain: Open from an unblocked machine, capture robots.txt and Terms, record whether it returns an officer name and whether it carries an 'as on' date. Seek written permission before any scraping (legal-ethics R6).
notes: Together with hyderabadpolice.gov.in/know_your_ps.html and the Passport Seva LocatePoliceStation tool, this is the canonical 'lookup, not dataset' shape for Indian police station directories.

name: Jharkhand Police 'Police Station Contacts' directory
publisher: Department of Police, Government of Jharkhand
caveats: EGRESS_BLOCKED (.gov.in) — page never opened
Per-district HTML table shape; no bulk export or API observed
No 'as on' date observed
evidence: URL and title 'Police Station Contacts | Department of Police, State Government of Jharkhand, India' returned by WebSearch. Page not opened.
how_to_obtain: Capture and read the ToU/robots pass; if reuse is permitted, a per-district HTML table is the cheapest route to station landlines and emails and avoids an RTI cycle.

name: Hyderabad City Police 'Know Your Police Station'
publisher: Hyderabad City Police, Telangana
caveats: EGRESS_BLOCKED (.gov.in) — page never opened
evidence: URL and title returned by WebSearch. Page not opened.
notes: Telangana already has police-station jurisdiction polygons (TRACGIS, via ramSeraph), so it is the best candidate for a full 'who polices here' surface once contact data is obtained.

name: Third-party republished Delhi SHO / Duty Officer contact lists
publisher: Various commercial and legal-services websites (sahodar.in, kksaxenaassociate.in, legalfree.in, Scribd uploads)
caveats: Unsourced, unlicensed, undated; multiple sites simultaneously claim to be the current '2026' list
Carry officers' personal mobile numbers and email ids
All EGRESS_BLOCKED; none opened
NOT ingestible and NOT a model — listed as market evidence and as a warning
evidence: Search results returned at least four distinct sites republishing 'All Delhi Police Station Name With SHO, DO Phone No' and 'List of SHO Email Ids of Delhi Police', including Scribd uploads and two SEO sites both claiming currency for 2026. Pages not opened.
notes: Evidence that demand for 'who do I contact' is real and is currently met badly. It is also the concrete picture of what our map would become if it published names: an undated snapshot competing with three other undated snapshots. The right response is to deep-link the force's own page, not to add a fifth copy.
how_to_obtain: Do not obtain and do not ingest. Recorded as market evidence only. If a copy is needed for the record, archive one page into research/_raw/ with a dated note that it is unlicensed and unsourced.

name: OpenStreetMap amenity=police in India — station phone/operator tags
publisher: OpenStreetMap Foundation / OSM India community
caveats: Coverage is a small fraction of reality: an independent harvester documents 'India has on the order of 17,000 police stations. OSM has a few thousand'
Strong urban bias: 'urban districts are well mapped, rural ones barely'
addr:district tagged on only ~3% of these nodes, so district must be assigned by point-in-polygon
Carries station phone/operator/website at best — NEVER an officer name
ODbL share-alike is a genuine consideration for derived products
All OSM hosts EGRESS_BLOCKED in this sandbox; coverage not measured directly
Overpass has strict fair-use limits — use a Geofabrik India .osm.pbf extract, do not harvest via Overpass at volume
evidence: Fetched raw.githubusercontent.com/AdItYa-1900/cyber-tools/main/scripts/gen_police_stations.py and read it in full. Its docstring states the coverage position quoted above verbatim, including 'There is no single public, machine-readable, complete national police station register.' Its extractor reads tags name/name:en/official_name, addr:housenumber/street/city/postcode/district/state, phone or contact:phone, operator, website or contact:website, and assigns state/district by ray-casting against Census-2011 district polygons from datameet/maps. OSM hosts probed 2026-09-20: openstreetmap.org, wiki, taginfo, overpass-api.de, download.geofabrik.de all returned connection failure (HTTP 000).
how_to_obtain: Geofabrik daily India .osm.pbf extract, filter amenity=police, then spatial-join to our ps_cd spine. Treat as a supplement for station phone only, never as a register.
notes: Useful for filling station landlines where the state publishes none. The verification grade refers to the harvester's documented findings, which were fetched and read; OSM itself was unreachable.

name: Data on Police Organisations (DoPO), annual
publisher: Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D), MHA
caveats: EGRESS_BLOCKED (.nic.in) — not opened
State-wise, not station-wise: gives counts of police stations, not a directory
Carries no officer particulars whatsoever
Sanctioned vs actual distinction matters and is easy to conflate
evidence: Search extracts: annual publication since 1986 covering manpower, infrastructure, vehicles and police stations for States/UTs/CPOs/CAPFs; 2023 datasets include state-wise numbers of police zones, ranges, districts, sub-divisions, circles and police stations as on 01.01.2023, and sanctioned vs actual police stations (rural, urban, special purpose). Pages not opened.
how_to_obtain: Download from an unblocked machine, or via dataful.in / indiastat mirrors of the same tables.
notes: The authoritative denominator for 'how many police stations does Bihar have', against which the 929 in INDIA_POLICE_STATIONS.geojson should be reconciled. Resolves the Patna 70-vs-75 discrepancy.

name: RTI finding: 50+ Bihar SHOs disciplined for sand/liquor mafia collusion (2022-2025)
publisher: RTI by Shiv Prakash Rai; reported by Deccan Chronicle
caveats: EGRESS_BLOCKED — article not opened; figure is from a search-result extract
'Suspended, transferred or formally charged' conflates three very different outcomes
Disciplinary action is not a finding of guilt
evidence: Search extract: 'over the past three years in Bihar, more than 50 Station House Officers... have faced disciplinary action for colluding with the very mafias they were supposed to dismantle. According to an RTI filed by activist Shiv Prakash Rai, over 50 SHOs across Bihar have been suspended, transferred, or formally charged for enabling the illegal sand and liquor trades.'
notes: Cuts both ways and is quoted in the dossier for that reason. It is the strongest evidence that person-level transparency produces accountability — and equally that the mechanism which produced it was a disciplinary record obtained by RTI, not a crime count on a map.
how_to_obtain: Open the article from an unblocked machine to confirm the figure, the period and the RTI's addressee. Better: re-file the underlying RTI to the Bihar DGP office for the disciplinary-action counts as aggregates by year and district, with no names.

name: Attacks on Bihar police by sand and liquor mafia; Bihar declared Naxal-free (Feb 2026)
publisher: Indian media (NewsClick, Amar Ujala, Deccan Herald, Tribune, NewsOnAir) reporting police/MHA statements
caveats: All sources EGRESS_BLOCKED; figures are search-result extracts
'50+ attacks in eleven months' is attributed to a Bihar Police ADG statement, period unspecified
The Naxal-free declaration is an MHA/state classification, not an absence of risk
evidence: Search extracts: Bihar Police ADG Sanjay Singh stated attacks on police have increased in connection with checking illegal sand and liquor trade; sand-mafia henchmen attacked police and administrative officials over 50 times in eleven months. 13 Sep 2026 (Amar Ujala, Samastipur/Darbhanga): liquor-mafia attack on an excise team injured a thanadhyaksh and several police personnel. Separately: Bihar declared Naxal-free after the surrender of the last armed Maoist in Munger (NewsOnAir, 19 Feb 2026); no Naxalite incident reported in Bihar in 2025, 220 Naxalites arrested; the 7 districts still classified LWE-affected nationally are Bijapur, Narayanpur, Sukma, Kanker, Dantewada (Chhattisgarh), West Singhbhum (Jharkhand) and Kandhamal (Odisha) — none in Bihar.
notes: Sharpens the officer-safety argument rather than inflating it. For Bihar the insurgency framing is largely spent; the live exposure is organised crime, and it bears on publishing a NAME plus a PERSONAL MOBILE joined to enforcement activity, not on publishing a station landline.
how_to_obtain: Open the cited articles from an unblocked machine to confirm the ADG attribution and the 'over 50 times in eleven months' figure and its period. The MHA LWE district classification should be confirmed against an MHA annual report.

name: UK Statistics Authority removal of National Statistics designation from police recorded crime (Jan 2014) and HMIC crime-recording inspection
publisher: UK Statistics Authority / Office for Statistics Regulation; HMIC; House of Commons PASC
caveats: Pages not opened — verified from search extracts only
A UK finding, cited as an analogy; India has no equivalent statistical regulator for police data
evidence: Search extracts: following a UK Statistics Authority assessment published January 2014, statistics based on police recorded crime data were found not to meet the standard for designation as National Statistics; the Authority set out 16 requirements. HMIC's 2014 national thematic report on crime recording found under-recording of crimes reported by victims at a level it called 'unacceptable'. The House of Commons Public Administration Select Committee reported under the title 'Caught red-handed: Why we can't count on Police Recorded Crime statistics'.
notes: The decisive methodological precedent for Part B. If performance pressure degraded police recorded crime in England and Wales badly enough to cost it its National Statistics designation, attaching a named individual station commander to his station's FIR count in India — where burking is already documented — would corrupt our own input data. This is the strongest argument against naming and it is not a legal one.

name: Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP (2013) and the persistence of burking; BNSS s.173(3)
publisher: Supreme Court of India; Parliament of India
caveats: indiankanoon.org and livelaw.in EGRESS_BLOCKED; judgment text not read
BNSS s.173(3) preliminary-enquiry window arguably widens police discretion not to register — verify against primary text
'Burking' is documented qualitatively; no national quantification was found
evidence: Search extracts: Lalita Kumari established that registration of an FIR is mandatory where information discloses a cognizable offence (CrPC s.154(1), which uses 'information' rather than 'credible information'). Commentary (Law School Policy Review, Mar 2026; The Criminal Law Blog) records that burking — active refusal or discouragement of FIR registration — persists as a systemic problem despite the mandate, and discusses the discrepancy between BNSS s.173(3) and Lalita Kumari. A LiveLaw headline records the Supreme Court observing that the Lalita Kumari judgment has been 'misused a lot' in a challenge to BNSS preliminary enquiry.
notes: Supplies the India-specific mechanism behind the UKSA analogy: the lever an SHO has to improve his station's apparent numbers is to register fewer FIRs, and that lever is already being pulled. It is also the reason the escalation panel (SDPO/SP/PCA/online-FIR/magistrate) is the right answer to the strongest objection against this dossier's recommendation.
how_to_obtain: Read Lalita Kumari on indiankanoon and BNSS s.173(3) on India Code from an unblocked machine before either is cited in published methodology copy.

name: Bihar police station jurisdiction polygons (i-Bhugoal, via Bharatmaps) — officer attributes unverified
publisher: Bihar i-Bhugoal / state GIS, republished by ramSeraph/indian_admin_boundaries and yashveeeeeeer/india-geodata
geo_coverage: Bihar (part of an 8-layer set: TN, KA, AP, TG, Bihar, RJ, Delhi, NCOG marine)

name: RTI drafts 5(f) office-and-contact directory and 5(g) changes of charge per station — extensions to rti-playbook.md
publisher: this project (research/sources/police-officers.md)
caveats: Untested — neither draft has been filed
Citizen-filer constraint applies (RTI s.3): a named Indian citizen must sign
5(g) depends on charge-handover records being retrievable per station; a s.7(9) refusal on cumulative burden is plausible for a whole-state ask
evidence: Drafted in this dossier from the evidence assembled here. Not filed, not tested against any PIO.
how_to_obtain: File 5(f) alongside existing draft 5(b) — both ask for offices, not persons, so neither is touched by RTI s.8(1)(j) as amended by DPDP s.44(3). File 5(g) separately, first in Bihar and one contrasting state, per the playbook's sequencing rule. In Bihar, name the Grih Darshan system and its field list explicitly to pre-empt s.7(9).
notes: 5(g) is the highest-value new ask: it yields a real per-station churn distribution and a direct measure of compliance with Prakash Singh Directive 3, while containing no personal data point at all. Nobody in India appears to publish it.
